entry.title: StVC 38: Markdown to Tutorial — Less Formatting | Stump the Vibe Coder Special Episode 38

media:group.media:title: StVC 38: Markdown to Tutorial — Less Formatting | Stump the Vibe Coder Special Episode 38
media:group.media:description:
Stump the Vibe Coder, Special Episode 38
Madeleine and I plan a Markdown-to-DOCX tool for my biostatistics tutorials. I would rather write the lesson once than fix the same spreadsheet reference in four places.
Source code: https://github.com/vosslab/markdown-to-tutorial
I start with the formatting problems in our existing tutorials: spreadsheet formulas, cell references, menu choices, and numbered parts and steps. We look at my exam-formatting and slide-building tools, create the new repository, and work through the requirements with Codex. The plan settles on one Markdown file containing readable instructions and worksheet tables, with DOCX, XLSX, and PDF outputs. Google Docs and Google Sheets are the intended classroom destinations, not something we verify on this stream.
Most of this episode is planning, not a finished-software demo. We revise the authoring format, get a written specification and implementation plan, and send Codex off to build the converter and adapt the existing tutorials. It is still working when we sign off. The repository linked above includes work completed after the recording.
Hosts: Neil Voss and Madeleine.
I'm Dr. Neil Voss, a biology professor at Roosevelt University. On Stump the Vibe Coder, I use AI coding assistants to work through science and teaching projects live. You do not need programming experience to follow along.
What part of preparing a class tutorial would you like to stop formatting by hand? Leave me a challenge in the comments.

media:group.media:description:
Stump the Vibe Coder, Episode 37
We built a game last week. This week, we get distracted playing it—and eventually start the next one.
Play Bad Cell Day: https://vosslab.github.io/bad-cell-day/ Bad Cell Day source: https://github.com/vosslab/bad-cell-day Plaque Attack source (build started near the end): https://github.com/vosslab/plaque-attack
Ayesha's Fireboy and Watergirl-inspired idea has grown into Bad Cell Day, a 58-level cooperative puzzle platformer starring Isp and Pac. We test its organ-themed levels, trade strategies for switches and moving platforms, and discover that Gem's bubble gun can be useful when it isn't getting in the way. Cana's boomerang is less popular. Controlling two characters on one keyboard remains a skill we are developing.
Owais's search for his keys becomes an AI-generated song, “Run Owais Run.” Later, Ayesha pitches a cardiovascular take on Bubble Trouble: bouncing cholesterol-themed hazards and a treatment-inspired arsenal. Jaren names it Plaque Attack. I turn the short pitch into a game specification, set up a TypeScript repository, and start the AI coding run. We leave that build running; this episode does not include a finished Plaque Attack playtest.
Hosts: Neil Voss, Ayesha Ahmed, Jaren Orbeck, and Owais, who joins for part of the episode.
I'm a biology professor with thirty-plus years of programming experience. My cohosts work in labs and are learning to code. On Stump the Vibe Coder, we try building science games, simulations, and lab tools with AI coding assistants—and come back to see whether they actually work.

entry.title: StVC 36: Bad Cell Day — Two Drugs, One Keyboard | Stump the Vibe Coder Episode 36

media:group.media:title: StVC 36: Bad Cell Day — Two Drugs, One Keyboard | Stump the Vibe Coder Episode 36
media:group.media:description:
Stump the Vibe Coder, Episode 36
Two drug-inspired heroes need teamwork. We need to remember which keys move which one.
Project: https://vosslab.github.io/bad-cell-day/ Repository: https://github.com/vosslab/bad-cell-day
Ayesha brings us a pharmaceutical twist on Fireboy and Watergirl: two characters with different abilities who need each other to reach their goal. We turn that idea into Bad Cell Day, a cooperative puzzle platformer starring Isp and Pac, and hand the TypeScript build to our AI coding assistants. Naming the game is easy compared with pronouncing the drugs.
We get a playable prototype onto GitHub Pages, then Jaren takes on both characters with one keyboard while the rest of us offer highly qualified advice. Shared switches, color-coded barriers, and uneven difficulty give us plenty to debug. We reshape the characters around molecular structures, ask for pink tissue and a little body horror, and leave more work for the agents overnight. This is a playful drug-inspired game, not a simulation of treatment or a claim about clinical effectiveness.
Along the way we revisit Steroid Quest and Nobel Combat, argue with AI-generated thumbnails that do not look like us, and finish with drug chemistry and biotech movie ideas. The linked game may include improvements made after this recording.
Hosts: Neil Voss, Ayesha Ahmed, Jaren Orbeck, Owais
On Stump the Vibe Coder, we turn science questions, educational games, and lab ideas into live builds with AI coding assistants. I bring decades of programming experience; our lab-science cohosts bring the challenges and learn to code as we go. Sometimes we get a working game. Sometimes we find out what needs fixing.

entry.title: StVC 35: Steroid Quest — Can a Steroid Reach the DNA? | Stump the Vibe Coder Episode 35

media:group.media:title: StVC 35: Steroid Quest — Can a Steroid Reach the DNA? | Stump the Vibe Coder Episode 35
media:group.media:description:
Stump the Vibe Coder, Episode 35
Can we turn steroid signaling into an arcade game? We send a steroid hormone through the cell, into the nucleus, and toward its receptor and DNA target while Codex builds the route live.
Project: https://vosslab.github.io/steroid-quest-into-the-nucleus/ Repository: https://github.com/vosslab/steroid-quest-into-the-nucleus
We start with the old mobile game Bounce and ask how to move that mechanic into biochemistry. The answer becomes Steroid Quest: a side-scrolling molecular platformer where a steroid crosses the membrane, navigates the cytoplasm, finds a nuclear pore, reaches its receptor, and heads for DNA. We deliberately choose arcade challenge over a formal lesson—and make it harder than our recent games.
While Codex builds the prototype, we take a detour to make the thoroughly unnecessary Suno song “Run, Binay, Run.” Jaren then playtests the game, reaches the nucleus, and discovers a carrier-protein power-up that enables double jumping. The test also exposes what still needs work: the cytoplasm section runs long, the collectibles are unclear, movement feels heavy, and some organelles need better art. The final visual revision is pushed near the end but is not fully replay-tested on stream.
The live build uses TypeScript, SolidJS, and Phaser 3. The linked project has continued to evolve since the recording and now uses a custom Canvas 2D game layer. It is a stylized arcade interpretation of steroid signaling, not a literal biological simulation.
Hosts: Neil Voss, Ayesha Ahmed, Jaren Orbeck, Owais, Binay
New here? Stump the Vibe Coder brings an experienced programmer and coding newcomers from science labs together to build software with AI, live—then test, debug, and sometimes derail it with a bad AI song. entry.title: StVC 34: Nobel Combat — Great Song, Questionable Fighting | Stump the Vibe Coder Episode 34

media:group.media:title: StVC 34: Nobel Combat — Great Song, Questionable Fighting | Stump the Vibe Coder Episode 34
media:group.media:description:
Stump the Vibe Coder, Episode 34
We want Nobel Prize winners to fight each other, with their discoveries as special moves. I ask the AI for better-looking characters. They disappear. Meanwhile, a question about my skincare routine turns into a song about an undead biochemist. This is Nobel Combat.
Project: https://vosslab.github.io/nobel-combat/ Repository: https://github.com/vosslab/nobel-combat
Ayesha, Jaren, Owais, and I give 3D another try with Babylon.js and Codex. We start with Otto Heinrich Warburg, argue about the roster, and decide Rosalind Franklin deserves a secret character slot even though she never received a Nobel Prize. The goal is a fun fighting game. The AI would first like us to answer several more planning questions.
Our first playable duel has stiff red and blue fighters, a camera we can't figure out, and some very questionable punching. At one point I am getting beaten up by a character I can't even see. We keep changing the camera and movement, then try open character assets. That brings its own entertainment: loading errors, uncooperative arms, and a complaint about red eyebrows. By the end we can test punches and a movable camera, but the scientist identities and research-inspired powers are still work to do.
While the agents work, we make a Suno song about my apparently suspicious height, skincare, and windowless office. The tallest undead biochemist gets a sequel before the fighters get sorted out. Sometimes the song is the better project. If you want the first game test, jump to 37:32; the song-making starts at 21:54.
The linked game has improved substantially since this recording, including its scientist roster and special moves. This episode shows the rough original build, not all the features you can play today.

entry.title: StVC 33: Fold Spacer — Racing Through Proteins | Stump the Vibe Coder Episode 33

media:group.media:title: StVC 33: Fold Spacer — Racing Through Proteins | Stump the Vibe Coder Episode 33
media:group.media:description:
Stump the Vibe Coder, Episode 33
Can we turn a flight through a real protein structure into a three-lane arcade runner? We take Fold Spacer for a spin—and discover that dodging side chains is harder when we can't tell which lane they're in.
Play the current project: https://vosslab.github.io/Fold-Spacer/ Source code: https://github.com/vosslab/Fold-Spacer Original Fold Spacer by Martin Steinegger: https://github.com/martin-steinegger/Fold-Spacer
Jaren, Owais, and I start with an open-source protein flight demo and try Owais's idea: give it a Subway Surfers-style lane system. We fork Fold Spacer, ask Codex to plan the redesign, and work through TypeScript, Rust/WebAssembly, and WebGL choices while keeping the protein structure as the game world.
The session also includes a return to Ms Taq Man, Jaren's Meta Quest workspace demonstration, arcade and VR talk, and an extended AI-song detour for Ayesha.
We get a playable three-lane version onto GitHub Pages and try an updated build with a ghost-like guide. But lane readability, collision feedback, and timing still leave us confused. The session ends with the coding credits running out and a game we can build on—not a polished final release. The linked project has continued to develop since this recording.
Hosts: Neil Voss, Jaren Orbeck, Owais

media:group.media:title: StVC 32: Ms Taq Man — Trapped in the PCR Maze | Stump the Vibe Coder Episode 32
media:group.media:description:
Stump the Vibe Coder, Episode 32
Can AI turn PCR into a playable arcade game before the livestream ends? Neil, Ayesha, Jaren, and Owais build Ms Taq Man live, then discover that their DNA-copying maze is nearly impossible to finish.
Play the project: https://vosslab.github.io/ms-taq-man/ Source code: https://github.com/vosslab/ms-taq-man
The team turns Taq polymerase into an arcade hero that collects primers and synthesizes DNA through a Pac-Man-style maze. Coding agents produce a TypeScript browser prototype, but the real work begins during the playtest: fixing an impossible 100% coverage rule, deploying updates, chasing collision bugs, and polishing the music, CRT scanlines, power-ups, and denaturation animation until players can clear thermal cycles.
Ms Taq Man is a stylized molecular-biology arcade game rather than a literal PCR simulation.

entry.title: StVC 31: Cancer Clicker — From One Cell to a Colony | Stump the Vibe Coder Episode 31

media:group.media:title: StVC 31: Cancer Clicker — From One Cell to a Colony | Stump the Vibe Coder Episode 31
media:group.media:description:
Stump the Vibe Coder, Episode 31
Neil, Jaren, and Owais turn a cancer-cell growth concept into Cancer Clicker, a browser game about harvesting resources, buying mutations, and building a strange cell colony.
Play the project: https://vosslab.github.io/cancer-clicker/ Source code: https://github.com/vosslab/cancer-clicker
The team first revisits Attack on Cancer and its upgraded CRISPR, chemotherapy, immune-cell, and radiation towers, then checks progress on a virtual cell-culture lab. For the main build, they ask Codex to make a TypeScript resource-management game in which a transformed cell gathers nutrients, energy, and biomass to expand through its host.
The first Tumor Tycoon prototype feels more like Cookie Clicker, so the design is simplified and renamed Cancer Clicker. They test visible mutation upgrades, immune pressure, host control, and the final playable loop—with a few AI-generated songs filling the build time.
Cancer Clicker is a stylized, non-clinical strategy toy, not medical guidance or a prediction of real cancer outcomes.

media:group.media:title: StVC 30: Attack on Cancer — Can Our Defenses Hold? | Stump the Vibe Coder Episode 30
media:group.media:description:
Stump the Vibe Coder, Episode 30
Jaren brought us a challenge: Bloons Tower Defense, but with cancer cells. So we built it live with AI. Then I told it the challenge should be more challenging. We eventually died on the first round.
Project: https://vosslab.github.io/attack-on-cancer/ Repository: https://github.com/vosslab/attack-on-cancer
This is Attack on Cancer, one of our better games. We defend a tissue route with doctors, chemotherapy, cytotoxic T cells, radiation bots, and antibody therapy. Apparently, quite a few of them shoot lasers.
Getting there takes a while. Codex keeps asking planning questions, I explain bikeshedding, and we play Glycolysis Okimon and Super Bowling while the agents work. Eventually we have a game to test instead of more questions to answer.
We add clearer attacks, sound effects, faster waves, and a tumor-mass enemy. I enjoy the new sounds for a bit before finding out nobody else can hear them. Then we keep adjusting the difficulty until our defenses stop looking so impressive. We get the game onto GitHub Pages and finish with ideas for another map and tower upgrades.
This recording is the original build and playtest; we've kept working on the linked game since then. It's a stylized biology game, not medical advice or a model of real treatment outcomes.

media:group.media:title: StVC 29: Glycolysis Okimon — From Speedrun to Biochem Quiz | Stump the Vibe Coder Episode 29
media:group.media:description:
Stump the Vibe Coder, Episode 29
Owais wants a Pokémon-style game. I have never played the originals, so naturally we're going to make one about glycolysis. Jaren speedruns our first version. Apparently, collecting the enzymes needs to involve a little more biochemistry.
Project: https://vosslab.github.io/glycolysis-okimon/ Repository: https://github.com/vosslab/glycolysis-okimon
We start with a trip through our old projects: my new Hermes assistant, some questionable bowling physics, molecular visualization, and a virtual lab that still needs a human touch. I manage a bowling score Jaren has never reached, mostly because my game has hundreds of pins. If you want to jump straight to the new build, start at 47:30.
Then we ask Codex to build Glycolysis Okimon, a top-down TypeScript adventure through a comic-book cell. You recruit the ten glycolysis enzymes and they follow you around. The first version is cute and very easy to finish. We add substrate questions and enzyme-choice encounters so there's something to figure out along the way. Jaren keeps speedrunning and looking for ways to break it. His monitor gets another song. Please respect the curve.
We get a playable version onto GitHub Pages and test it together. Near the end, a fresh build adds sound, an energy ledger, and a lipid-lockup enzyme puzzle. We still manage to argue about which enzyme cleaves what. Between builds, we take a fairly long detour through movies and the search for an available IMAX seat.
This recording shows the original build, including its rough edges. The linked game has continued changing since then; the current cofactor-collection systems and optional side quests are not all part of this stream.

entry.title: StVC 28: M.U.L.E. Remake — Robots, Resources, and Bugs | Stump the Vibe Coder Episode 28

media:group.media:title: StVC 28: M.U.L.E. Remake — Robots, Resources, and Bugs | Stump the Vibe Coder Episode 28
media:group.media:description:
Stump the Vibe Coder, Episode 28
We try to rebuild M.U.L.E. in the browser, brainstorm a cancer-cell version, and discover that passing tests doesn't mean the robot will move.
Project: https://vosslab.github.io/mule-game/ Repository: https://github.com/vosslab/mule-game
Jaren and I start with a look at the original M.U.L.E.: claim land, outfit robotic mules, produce resources, and trade at auction. The bigger idea is to turn that competition into a game about cancer cells competing for glucose, energy, and raw materials. We decide to build the ordinary economic game first, using TypeScript and AI coding assistance.
Owais joins partway through, and we work through the biology behind a possible adaptation, with detours into the Warburg effect, enzyme kinetics, and a substantial amount of AI songwriting. The cancer-cell version remains a concept during this stream. Its initial repository is https://github.com/vosslab/cancer-cell-mule .
By the final playtest, the browser prototype has land plots, mule purchases, and auction screens, but movement, placement, and production still need work. The linked project has developed since this recording; its current features are not all demonstrated here. This is the build session, including the parts that didn't work.

Can glycolysis become a rummy-style card game? We build a prototype, then discover that understanding the rules might be the harder challenge.
Project: https://vosslab.github.io/glycolysis-race-to-pyruvate/ Repository: https://github.com/vosslab/glycolysis-race-to-pyruvate
We turn glycolysis molecules, enzymes, and cofactors into playing cards and ask Codex to build a TypeScript browser game. The plan is to assemble pathway melds, keep track of ATP and other cofactors, and race toward pyruvate. The first interface needs more work—and even we struggle to explain how to play it.
While the agents work, we try biochemistry practice questions, revisit Science Career Survival and its possible scientific-misconduct outcomes, and make an increasingly elaborate AI song about Jaren's curved monitor. The response-time lyric needs a correction. Please note the decimal.
We finish with a rough glycolysis prototype, unclear rules, and an exhausted token budget. The final commit is still a promise at the close, not a demonstrated release. The linked game has continued to develop since this recording; its current interface and rules are not a claim about what worked on stream.

New here? Stump the Vibe Coder brings an experienced programmer and coding newcomers from science labs together to build software with AI, live. We try the result, find the confusing parts, and sometimes turn the conversation into an unnecessary song.

media:group.media:title: StVC 26: Pseudo-Code Mapper — Lost in the Plan | Stump the Vibe Coder Episode 26
media:group.media:description:
Stump the Vibe Coder, Episode 26
Can we turn a concept-map maker into a pseudo-code flowchart editor—or will our AI assistants spend the whole stream planning it?
Project: https://vosslab.github.io/pseudo-code-mapper/ Repository: https://github.com/vosslab/pseudo-code-mapper
My student Pierre and I set out to turn Concept Map Maker into Pseudo-Code Mapper: write an algorithm as text, then turn it into a flowchart. We revisit the existing concept-map tool and Pierre's study-site improvements before creating a separate repository from the starter code. GitHub's fork workflow gives us trouble, so we take the simpler route.
We design the text editor, decision diamonds, True/False branches, loop arrows, and pseudo-code grammar. The plan builds on TypeScript, SolidJS, Dagre, and SVG, with CodeMirror 6 selected for syntax highlighting. Claude drafts the plan, ChatGPT reviews it, and Codex takes a turn at implementation—but the plan and grammar keep getting revised while the app waits.
Near the end, I check what actually changed, fire Codex, and hand implementation back to Claude. The build is still incomplete when we wrap up. The linked editor was developed further after this recording; its current working features are not a finished app demonstrated on stream.
Hosts: Neil Voss, Pierre
New here? Stump the Vibe Coder brings an experienced programmer and students from science and computing together to build software with AI, live. You see the ideas, the debugging, and the occasions when planning takes longer than coding.
What short algorithm should we turn into a flowchart next—and where should its decisions or loops go? Suggest a concrete example or another challenge for us to build in the comments.
